segments.narration: An iron rod went through his head and he walked. Cavendish, Vermont, the thirteenth of September, 1848. Three foot seven of solid iron.
Phineas Gage was packing blasting powder when the charge went off early. The rod weighed thirteen pounds and passed clean through his skull.
He was talking within minutes. A doctor found him sitting in a chair outside the hotel half an hour later. How is that survivable?
John Harlow treated him, drained an abscess, and twenty years on wrote that friends said he was no longer Gage. That line built a legend.
Gage drove stagecoaches across Chile for years. Scans of his actual skull show only the left frontal lobe was hit.

verdicts.claim: John Martyn Harlow took charge of Gage's treatment, including draining an abscess, and published the account in which friends said he was no longer Gage only in 1868, after Gage's death.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: Harlow took charge around 6 pm, drained a later abscess, and published the no-longer-Gage account in 1868, after Gage's death; Simply Psychology notes Harlow's original account was later embellished.

verdicts.claim: Gage worked as a long-distance stagecoach driver on the Valparaiso to Santiago route in Chile from 1852, and CT studies of his actual skull concluded only the left frontal lobe was damaged.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives the 1852 move to Chile and the demanding Valparaiso to Santiago stagecoach work, and the Ratiu and Van Horn CT studies of the actual skull concluding the left frontal lobe was damaged and the right was not, correcting the 1994 Damasio study. Simply Psychology and Macmillan agree the damage was less extensive than popularly assumed.
